This is Turkey Dance. Ancient to present.
on_screen: Title card: Turkey Dance · United States · Ancient to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Turkey Dance is an ancient tradition with multiple origin stories, most notably that of a hunter who memorized the movements of wild turkeys.
Spanish missionaries in the 18th century recorded Hasinai women performing the dance to welcome returning warriors.
It has been maintained continuously by the Caddo people, with a notable resurgence in practice following World War II.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance is a celebration of Caddo survival and history.
It is the first dance performed during a day of tribal ceremonies.
It also serves to honor veterans, particularly during the concluding flag song and the lowering of the US flag at sunset.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance progresses through several phases.
Women move in a circular formation, which in the past centered on a pole.
In the third phase, dancers cluster around the male drummers in the center.
Watch for Turkey Mimicry.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Starts as a circle (formerly around a pole), moves to a central cluster around drummers

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Men perform the music, which consists of 52 specific songs sung in various Caddo dialects.
The primary instrumentation is the drum.
Listen for the Drum.
The sound is defined by male voices singing 52 traditional songs in Caddo dialects, accompanied by rhythmic drumming. The songs transition from creation myths to specific military histories.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Women wear ankle-length dresses with ribbon-trimmed skirts, matching blouses with flared yokes, and full-length aprons.
Key accessories include the dush-toh (a plaque with mirrors and ribbons), beadwork, and broadcloth blankets.
The dance traditionally occurs outdoors and must end by sunset.

scenes.title: The people
narration: While individual dancers are not named in the source, the Hasinay Society and the Caddo Cultural Club are identified as the primary organizations currently performing and preserving the dance.
The dance is currently centered in Binger, Oklahoma, at the Caddo National Tribal Complex.
The dance is a traditional indigenous American ceremonial dance.
